chunks.text:
## ADA Standards of Care — Glycemic Targets (Summary)

> **SOURCE:** American Diabetes Association, *Standards of Care in
> Diabetes — 2024*, Section 6 ("Glycemic Goals and Hypoglycemia").
> Published in *Diabetes Care*, Volume 47, Supplement 1.
> https://diabetesjournals.org/care/issue/47/Supplement_1
>
> **NOTICE:** Short factual summary for the AgentForge demo corpus.
> Not clinical advice. Refer to the source for the full guidance.

chunks.section: A1C Goal for Most Nonpregnant Adults
chunks.text:
## A1C Goal for Most Nonpregnant Adults

For many nonpregnant adults, an A1C goal of less than 7% is
reasonable. This target reduces the long-term risk of microvascular
complications (retinopathy, nephropathy, neuropathy) and, in
type 1 diabetes and early type 2 diabetes, macrovascular events.

The A1C goal should be individualized based on:

- **Duration of diabetes** — shorter durations support tighter targets
- **Life expectancy** — limited expectancy supports less stringent goals
- **Comorbid conditions** — extensive comorbidity supports less stringent goals
- **Established cardiovascular complications** — may support less stringent goals
- **Hypoglycemia unawareness** — less stringent goals reduce risk
- **Patient preferences and resources**

## Less Stringent A1C Goals

A1C goals less stringent than <7% (e.g., <8%) may be appropriate for
patients with:

- Limited life expectancy
- Advanced microvascular or macrovascular complications
- Extensive comorbid conditions
- Long-standing diabetes where the target has been difficult to
  achieve despite intensive efforts

## Glycemic Targets in Practice

For most nonpregnant adults with diabetes, the recommended targets are:

- **Preprandial (fasting) capillary plasma glucose:** 80–130 mg/dL
  (4.4–7.2 mmol/L)
- **Peak postprandial (1–2 hours after meal start) capillary plasma
  glucose:** less than 180 mg/dL (10.0 mmol/L)

## Hypoglycemia

Hypoglycemia is defined by glucose level alerts:

- **Level 1:** glucose 54–70 mg/dL (3.0–3.9 mmol/L) — alert value
- **Level 2:** glucose less than 54 mg/dL (less than 3.0 mmol/L) —
  clinically significant
- **Level 3:** severe event with cognitive impairment requiring
  external assistance

Avoiding level 2 and 3 hypoglycemia is essential for glycemic targets
to be considered safely achieved.

chunks.section: ACC/AHA 2017 Hypertension Guidelines — BP Categories and Targets (Summary)
chunks.text:
## ACC/AHA 2017 Hypertension Guidelines — BP Categories and Targets (Summary)

> **SOURCE:** Whelton PK, Carey RM, Aronow WS, et al. *2017
> ACC/AHA/AAPA/ABC/ACPM/AGS/APhA/ASH/ASPC/NMA/PCNA Guideline for the
> Prevention, Detection, Evaluation, and Management of High Blood
> Pressure in Adults*. Hypertension. 2018;71(6):e13–e115.
>
> **NOTICE:** Short factual summary for the AgentForge demo corpus.
> Not clinical advice. Refer to the source for the full guidance.

## Blood Pressure Categories (in mmHg)

The 2017 ACC/AHA guideline classifies adult BP into four categories
based on the higher of systolic (SBP) or diastolic (DBP):

| Category               | SBP        |     | DBP       |
|------------------------|------------|-----|-----------|
| Normal                 | <120       | and | <80       |
| Elevated               | 120–129    | and | <80       |
| Hypertension Stage 1   | 130–139    | or  | 80–89     |
| Hypertension Stage 2   | ≥140       | or  | ≥90       |

A diagnosis of hypertension is made when the average of two or more
properly measured readings on two or more occasions falls into stage
1 or stage 2 categories.

## Treatment Targets

For most adults with hypertension and confirmed BP ≥130/80 mmHg, the
target is **<130/80 mmHg**.

Stratification by 10-year ASCVD risk:

- **Stage 1 hypertension (130–139/80–89) without ASCVD or 10-year
  ASCVD risk ≥10%:** lifestyle therapy first; reassess in 3–6 months.
- **Stage 1 hypertension with clinical ASCVD or 10-year ASCVD risk
  ≥10%, or with diabetes / CKD:** lifestyle therapy *plus*
  pharmacologic therapy.
- **Stage 2 hypertension (≥140/≥90):** lifestyle therapy plus
  pharmacologic therapy in all adults.

## First-Line Pharmacologic Options

Initial first-line therapy for non-Black adults includes:

- Thiazide diuretics
- Calcium channel blockers
- ACE inhibitors or ARBs (do NOT combine ACEi with ARB)

For Black adults without HF or CKD, initial therapy includes
thiazides or CCBs.

## Special Populations

- **Patients with CKD (stage 3 or higher, or stage 1–2 with
  albuminuria):** ACE inhibitors or ARBs are preferred.
- **Patients with diabetes:** any of the four classes is acceptable;
  ACEi/ARB if albuminuria is present.
- **Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction:** GDMT (e.g.,
  ACEi/ARB/ARNI plus beta blocker plus aldosterone antagonist).

## Out-of-Office Confirmation

Before initiating pharmacotherapy for newly diagnosed stage 1
hypertension, confirmation by out-of-office BP measurements (home BP
monitoring or 24-hour ambulatory BP monitoring) is recommended to
avoid white-coat misclassification.

chunks.section: Hemoglobin A1C — Diagnostic and Interpretive Notes (Summary)
chunks.text:
## Hemoglobin A1C — Diagnostic and Interpretive Notes (Summary)

> **SOURCE:** American Diabetes Association *Standards of Care in
> Diabetes — 2024*, Section 2 ("Diagnosis and Classification of
> Diabetes"). Diabetes Care 47(Supplement_1).
>
> **NOTICE:** Short factual summary for the AgentForge demo corpus.
> Not clinical advice. Refer to the source for the full guidance.

## A1C as a Diagnostic Test

A1C is one of four equivalent diagnostic criteria for diabetes:

- **A1C ≥6.5%** (NGSP-certified, DCCT-aligned assay)
- Fasting plasma glucose ≥126 mg/dL (7.0 mmol/L) — fasting ≥8 hours
- 2-hour PG ≥200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L) during 75-g OGTT
- Random plasma glucose ≥200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L) with classic
  symptoms of hyperglycemia

Unless there is unequivocal hyperglycemia, the diagnosis requires
two abnormal test results — either two of the same test on separate
days, or two different tests at the same visit.

## Diagnostic Categories

| Category               | A1C            | FPG (mg/dL)        | 2-hr PG (mg/dL)    |
|------------------------|----------------|--------------------|--------------------|
| Normal                 | <5.7%          | <100               | <140               |
| Prediabetes            | 5.7–6.4%       | 100–125 (IFG)      | 140–199 (IGT)      |
| Diabetes               | ≥6.5%          | ≥126               | ≥200               |

Prediabetes is a risk state, not a milder disease — adults with
prediabetes should be counseled on lifestyle modification and
monitored annually.

## When NOT to Use A1C

A1C is unreliable in conditions affecting RBC turnover or hemoglobin
structure. Use plasma glucose instead in:

- Hemoglobinopathies (sickle cell disease/trait, HbC, HbE, HbS-β
  thalassemia)
- Recent significant blood loss or transfusion
- Hemolytic anemia
- Iron-deficiency anemia (under-treated)
- Erythropoietin therapy or iron repletion
- Pregnancy (second and third trimester) — use OGTT
- End-stage renal disease — A1C may underestimate
- Recent severe hyperglycemia (the A1C lags by ~3 months)

## Interpretive Notes for the Agent

- **A1C trends matter as much as absolute values.** A patient moving
  from 6.4% to 7.5% over 6 months has worsening control even though
  both are "abnormal" — surface the trajectory, not just the latest
  result.
- **A1C must be interpreted alongside CBC.** Anemia (any cause) can
  shift A1C up or down; surface concurrent CBC results when
  available.
- **A new A1C ≥9% with prior values <7% is a meaningful clinical
  change** — escalate.

## AHA/ACC 2018 Cholesterol Guidelines — Statin Therapy (Summary)

> **SOURCE:** Grundy SM, Stone NJ, Bailey AL, et al. *2018
> AHA/ACC/AACVPR/AAPA/ABC/ACPM/ADA/AGS/APhA/ASPC/NLA/PCNA Guideline
> on the Management of Blood Cholesterol*. Circulation.
> 2019;139(25):e1082–e1143.
>
> **NOTICE:** Short factual summary for the AgentForge demo corpus.
> Not clinical advice. Refer to the source for the full guidance.

## Four Major Statin Benefit Groups

The 2018 guideline identifies four groups for whom statin therapy is
recommended:

1. **Adults with clinical ASCVD** (acute coronary syndromes, history
   of MI, stable or unstable angina, coronary or other arterial
   revascularization, stroke, TIA, or peripheral arterial disease).
2. **Adults aged ≥21 with primary severe LDL-C ≥190 mg/dL**.
3. **Adults aged 40–75 with diabetes and LDL-C 70–189 mg/dL**.
4. **Adults aged 40–75 without diabetes, with LDL-C 70–189 mg/dL,
   and 10-year ASCVD risk ≥7.5%** based on the Pooled Cohort
   Equations.

## Intensity of Statin Therapy

| Intensity     | Expected LDL-C reduction | Examples                           |
|---------------|--------------------------|------------------------------------|
| High          | ≥50%                     | Atorvastatin 40–80 mg, Rosuvastatin 20–40 mg |
| Moderate      | 30–49%                   | Atorvastatin 10–20 mg, Rosuvastatin 5–10 mg, Simvastatin 20–40 mg |
| Low           | <30%                     | Simvastatin 10 mg, Pravastatin 10–20 mg |

## Treatment Recommendations

- **Clinical ASCVD, age ≤75:** high-intensity statin (or maximum
  tolerated intensity).
- **Clinical ASCVD, age >75:** moderate- or high-intensity statin
  after risk discussion.
- **Primary severe LDL-C ≥190:** high-intensity statin without
  10-year risk assessment.
- **Diabetes, age 40–75:** moderate-intensity statin; add high-
  intensity if multiple ASCVD risk enhancers.
- **Primary prevention, age 40–75, ASCVD risk 7.5–<20%:** moderate-
  intensity statin after risk discussion.
- **Primary prevention, age 40–75, ASCVD risk ≥20%:** high-intensity
  statin to reduce LDL-C ≥50%.

## Risk Enhancers

Risk enhancers that may favor statin therapy in borderline cases
include:

- Family history of premature ASCVD
- Persistently elevated LDL-C ≥160 mg/dL
- Chronic kidney disease
- Metabolic syndrome
- Conditions specific to women (preeclampsia, premature menopause)
- Inflammatory diseases (psoriasis, rheumatoid arthritis, HIV)
- Ethnicity (e.g., South Asian)
- Persistently elevated triglycerides ≥175 mg/dL
- ABI <0.9, hs-CRP ≥2.0 mg/L, Lp(a) ≥50 mg/dL, apoB ≥130 mg/dL

## Coronary Artery Calcium

In adults age 40–75 at borderline (5 to <7.5%) or intermediate
(≥7.5 to <20%) 10-year ASCVD risk where the decision is uncertain,
measuring CAC may help refine risk:

- **CAC = 0:** withholding statin therapy is reasonable (unless
  diabetes, family history of premature CHD, or smoking).
- **CAC 1–99:** statin therapy is favored, especially for those age
  ≥55.
- **CAC ≥100 or ≥75th percentile:** statin therapy is indicated.

chunks.section: KDIGO CKD Staging — GFR and Albuminuria Categories (Summary)
chunks.text:
## KDIGO CKD Staging — GFR and Albuminuria Categories (Summary)

> **SOURCE:** *KDIGO 2024 Clinical Practice Guideline for the
> Evaluation and Management of Chronic Kidney Disease*. Kidney
> International Supplements. https://kdigo.org/guidelines/ckd/
>
> **NOTICE:** Short factual summary for the AgentForge demo corpus.
> Not clinical advice. Refer to the source for the full guidance.

## Definition

CKD is defined as abnormalities of kidney structure or function,
present for **>3 months**, with implications for health.

Diagnostic criteria require ≥1 of:

- GFR <60 mL/min/1.73 m² for >3 months
- Markers of kidney damage (one or more):
  - Albuminuria (AER ≥30 mg/24h or ACR ≥30 mg/g)
  - Urine sediment abnormalities
  - Electrolyte and other abnormalities due to tubular disorders
  - Histologic abnormalities
  - Structural abnormalities on imaging
  - History of kidney transplantation

## GFR Categories

| Category | GFR (mL/min/1.73 m²) | Description                       |
|----------|----------------------|-----------------------------------|
| G1       | ≥90                  | Normal or high                    |
| G2       | 60–89                | Mildly decreased                  |
| G3a      | 45–59                | Mildly to moderately decreased    |
| G3b      | 30–44                | Moderately to severely decreased  |
| G4       | 15–29                | Severely decreased                |
| G5       | <15                  | Kidney failure                    |

GFR categories alone do not define CKD without markers of damage —
G1 and G2 require an additional marker (e.g., albuminuria).

## Albuminuria Categories

| Category | ACR (mg/g) | ACR (mg/mmol) | Description                  |
|----------|------------|---------------|------------------------------|
| A1       | <30        | <3            | Normal to mildly increased   |
| A2       | 30–300     | 3–30          | Moderately increased         |
| A3       | >300       | >30           | Severely increased           |

The preferred specimen is a **first-morning void**, with quantitative
albumin-to-creatinine ratio (ACR) reported. Random spot collections
are acceptable when first-morning void isn't available.

## Combined Risk Stratification

Risk of progression and adverse outcomes is stratified by the
combination of GFR and albuminuria:

- **Low risk:** G1–G2 with A1 (and no other markers)
- **Moderately increased risk:** G1–G2 with A2; G3a with A1
- **High risk:** G1–G2 with A3; G3a with A2; G3b with A1
- **Very high risk:** G3a with A3; G3b with A2 or A3; G4–G5 with any

Higher-risk categories are referred to nephrology and warrant more
frequent monitoring.

## Practical Notes

- The GFR equation recommended is the **2021 CKD-EPI creatinine
  equation** (not race-corrected). The cystatin C equation is
  preferred when greater accuracy is needed.
- A single low GFR is not CKD — confirm chronicity (>3 months) before
  staging.
- Albuminuria progression and stable GFR can both indicate
  progressive CKD; track BOTH markers over time.
